en: Now begins the hymn of one hundred and eight names of Śrī Sītā, contained within the glorious Ānanda-Rāmāyaṇa.
Agastya said:
Thus, O Sutīkṣṇa, this armor (kavaca) of Sītā has been declared by me to you.
Hereafter, listen to another, the supreme hymn (stotra) of Sītā.
In this [work] there are indeed one hundred and eight names of Sītā;
this hymn of one hundred and eight names of Sītā is unsurpassed.
Those men who recite it here find their existence fruitful.
Those men are blessed in the world; they indeed go to Vaikuṇṭha.
[End of] Nyāsa. Of this Śrī Sītā-nāmāṣṭottara-śata-mantra...
Agastya is the seer;
Anuṣṭubh is the meter;
Rama is the seed-syllable.
*Mātuliṅgī* is the *śakti*;
*padmākṣajā* is the *kīlaka*;
*avanijā* is the *astra*.
"Janakajā" is the armor;
"Mūlakāsura-mardinī" is the supreme mantra.
[Recited] for the sake of pleasing Śrī Sītārāmacandra and for the sake of accomplishing all desires.
This is the application for the recitation.
The ritual placement upon the hands (kara-nyāsa).
Oṃ, salutation to Sītā with the two thumbs; Oṃ, salutation to Ramā with the two index fingers;
Oṃ, salutation to Mātuliṅgī with the two middle fingers.
Oṃ, homage to Padmākṣajā with the two ring fingers; Oṃ, homage to Avanijā with the two little fingers;
Oṃ, homage to Janakajā with the palms and backs of the hands.
The ritual placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
Oṃ, obeisance to Sītā, the heart; Oṃ, svāhā to Ramā, the head;
Oṃ, vaṣaṭ to Mātuliṅgī, the tuft of hair.
Oṃ, to Padmākṣajā, the three eyes, vauṣaṭ!
Oṃ, to Janakātmajā, the weapon, phaṭ!
Oṃ, to Mūlakāsuramardinī—thus is the binding of the directions (digbandha).
Now, meditation.
O Lord of Brahmins, she who dwells upon the beautiful left side of the Leader of the Raghus— she who is radiant, whose eyes are lovely, whose face protects the Brahmins,
who is clothed in garments shining like a mass of lightning, and who shatters the suffering of her devotees.
May she, whose eyes are fixed upon the pair of glorious Rāghava’s lotus feet, protect [us].
The illustrious Sītā, daughter of Janaka, princess of Videha, beloved of Rāghava; the goddess Ramā, daughter of the Earth, the beautiful one who brought about the end of the Rākṣasas;
she who is protected by jewels, the bearer of the citron fruit, the daughter of Mithilā, who grants satisfaction to her devotees.
Born from the lotus-seed, with lotus-eyes, a smiling face, and the sound of anklets;
residing in Vaikuṇṭha, she is Śrī, the giver of liberation and the fulfiller of desires;
the daughter of the king, golden-hued, with tender limbs and sweet speech.
Kuśāmbikā, the divine giver, the mother of Lava, the enchanting Manoharā; she whose feet are saluted by Hanumān, the charming one, the wearer of armlets;
she who dwells in the midst of the Aśoka grove, the deluder of Rāvaṇa and the others.
Seated upon a celestial chariot, she of beautiful eyebrows and lovely hair, adorned with a girdle;
she who is the form of passion (rajas), the form of activity (sattva), and the form of darkness (tamas), dwelling in fire;
her mind attached to the golden deer, she who dwells in the hermitage of Vālmīki.
Devoted to her husband, Mahāmāyā was dressed in yellow silk;
she had eyes like those of a deer, lips like the bimba fruit, and was highly skilled in the science of archery.
Of gentle appearance, the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha was fanned with a yak-tail whisk.
Sumedhā, the daughter of divine form, the protectress of the three worlds; Annapūrṇā, Mahālakṣmī, Dhī, Lajjā, and Sarasvatī;
Śānti, Puṣṭi, Śamā, Gaurī, and Prabhā—the dweller in Ayodhyā.
Vasantaśīlatā, Gaurī, she whose mind is satisfied by bathing,
Ramā, Bhadrasaṃsthā, she whose breasts are golden jars;
Surārcitā, Dhṛti, Kānti, Smṛti, Medhā, and Vibhāvarī.
She has a slender waist, possesses beautiful hips, and is adorned with golden bracelets;
she delights Rāghava by offering her own ornaments to the wives of the twice-born,
is devoted to the service of Śrī Rāma, and wears jeweled earrings.
She who rests upon the left side of Rāma, the sole delight of Rāmacandra;
she who sports in the waters of the Sarayū, the enchantress of Rāma;
(13) she who is like gold, meritorious, of holy fame, and possessed of all arts.
She has a melodious voice, a neck like a conch shell, thighs like plantain stalks, and the gait of an elephant.
Her mind is dedicated to Rāma; she is praised by Rāma and beloved by Rāma.
Her body is marked with the signs of Śrī Rāma’s feet, and she constantly utters, "Rāma, Rāma."
Reclining on Rāma’s couch, the excellent one who washes Rāma’s feet,
unsatisfied even by the food of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu), holding a citron (mātuliṅga) in her hand;
established in divine sandalwood paste, she is the crusher of the demon Śrīmūlaka.
Thus, those men on earth who recite this most meritorious hymn of one hundred and eight names of Sītā are blessed and destined for heaven;
this hymn of one hundred and eight names of Sītā is supreme.
O Brahmin, there are many great and merit-bestowing hymns in Japan that should always be recited with effort and devotion;
yet none of them here are equal to this one.

And this is the best among hymns, bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men. Thus, O Sutīṣṇa, I have declared to you these one hundred and eight auspicious names of Sītā, which grant merit and bestow blessings upon hearing them.

This should be recited with effort by men upon rising in the morning, and also at the time of the worship of Sītā; it bestows all that is desired. Thus ends [the section] from the glorious *Śatakoṭi Rāmacarita*.
The hymn of one hundred and eight names of Sītā from the enchanting Kāṇḍa of the glorious Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa is complete.
